### Observed differences

- In the later window, six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22) are handled by a largely different set of resources. Earlier, a stable group of resources each held roughly 4–11 in 100 events on each of these activities (User_46 alone held about 7–11 in 100 on all six); later, most of that group drops out of the leading positions or falls to about 5 in 100, while a different group takes over — User_39's share rose in every one of these activities (on A22 from about 7 to about 13 in 100 events). The profile differences are large (0.29–0.37 cosine dissimilarity) and each exceeds those of all but about 1 in 2,000 random re-splits, while participation stayed flat (A01 appears in 200 of 200 traces in both windows, A22 in 133 of 200). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- A10 changed from concentrated to dispersed handling: earlier, User_117 handled about 17 in 100 events and the ten most frequent resources together about 86 in 100, leaving about 14 in 100 for everyone else; later, the leading resources' shares roughly halved (User_117 to about 10 in 100) and the share going to resources beyond the leading group rose to about 52 in 100. [ASSIGN003]
- The elapsed time between consecutive completions of A09 and A04 shows a slightly higher and much heavier-tailed distribution in the later window: the mean roughly doubled (about 0.017 to 0.032 hours, i.e., roughly 1 to 2 minutes) while the median moved only from about 0.016 to 0.020 hours and the spread grew from about 0.005 to 0.116 hours; such consecutive pairs also became less frequent (132 to 105, about 66 to 53 per 100 traces). [TWAIT001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a change in resource allocation: in the later window, work on A01, A03, A10, A13, A14, A17 and A22 is handled by a largely different group of resources than before — resources that previously each covered roughly 4–11 in 100 events (including User_46) largely leave the leading positions, a different group including User_39 takes over, and A10's previously concentrated handling spreads out, with about half of its events going to resources beyond the leading group. This rests on direct allocation evidence: the resources family produced 7 qualifying items where about 0.007 would qualify by chance (roughly a thousandfold excess), all items point in the same direction, each difference beats all but about 1 in 2,000 random re-splits, and 133–270 traces per window stand behind each profile while participation itself did not change. The same newly prominent resources recur across activities, suggesting one coordinated reallocation; the seven items therefore likely describe a single underlying difference (A13 and A14 even have identical profiles) rather than independent confirmations. Control-flow indicators produced no qualifying items (0 against about 0.17 expected), so no structural change accompanies the reallocation in this evidence. Limitations: the resource codes are anonymous and the evidence shows only that shares moved; a shift in the mix of cases reaching these activities, rather than a change in the allocation itself, cannot be ruled out. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

Other differences: the A09–A04 elapsed-time distribution has a higher mean and a much heavier tail in the later window (mean about 0.017 to 0.032 hours). As the only time item, against about 0.015 expected by chance, it is compatible with an unchanged process and does not by itself establish a change in timing. [TWAIT001]
